title: Find your place
summary: A terminal displays a shell, which reads commands. pwd prints the directory you are currently using.
introduction: A terminal displays a shell, which reads commands. pwd prints the directory you are currently using. We will use a small example so you can follow each step.
learningObjectives: Use the example to answer a practice question

blocks.text: A terminal displays a shell, which reads commands. pwd prints the directory you are currently using.

blocks.title: Before you start
blocks.text: Use a Linux terminal or a suitable practice environment. Commands shown here do not run inside this frontend website. Work only with your own practice files; no administrator commands are needed.
This course teaches the basics. It does not cover every feature of Linux. Keep real personal data and secret keys out of practice files.
The output is the path of your current directory. It differs between computers.

items: Read the example from top to bottom. Point to the part that uses the new idea.
Write down your current path before changing folders.
Explain what changed in your own words. Check the example again if you get stuck.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: A terminal command acts in its current directory unless you give another path.
For more detail later, use this [Linux further reading](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html).

seo.title: Linux: Find your place
seo.description: Learn about find your place in Linux. Follow a small example, understand the result, and practise with a clear question.
